squatter_eviction_en:
In Spain, the clock on a squatted home starts the moment someone enters, and 48 hours later everything changes.

Inside that window, police can remove occupants without a court date, as long as you can prove the property is yours. Past it, the case goes to court: you hire a lawyer, file for eviction and prove ownership with deeds, photos of you in the home, flight tickets, even neighbour statements. The squatters then get to argue their own claim or show they are paying to stay. Only when a judge sets a date can police remove them by force.

Whatever you do, do not change the locks, block re-entry or confront them. Spanish law can turn that against you. Depending on the region, a court eviction can take 18 months to 2 years, though many cases resolve much faster. If you find occupants, report it to the police the same day.

squatter_prevention_en:
Squatters in Spain rarely pick homes at random. They pick homes that look abandoned.

The 48 hour rule makes discovery speed the whole game: police can evict without a court order only if occupation is caught within 48 hours of entry. So prevention is really detection. An alarm system connected to the police both deters entry and timestamps it, keeping you inside that critical window. Automated systems, lights that switch on and blinds that rise, make the house read as occupied through the low season, when most squatting goes unnoticed.

A trusted neighbour who collects post and waters plants adds a human check and makes the home look lived in. Renting the property out while you are away brings income and means any occupation is found within the first 48 hours. Before you next leave, stand on the street and ask what your house signals to a stranger.

squatter_insurance_en:
There is insurance in Spain for one specific nightmare: someone else living in your house.

Many providers offer property insurance with illegal occupation cover, and it is often well priced. Why it matters: once squatters pass the 48 hour mark, removal becomes a court process that can take between 18 months and 2 years depending on where in Spain the property sits. Through that whole period, the home is out of your hands and the costs keep landing on you. Occupation cover helps with the financial losses built up while the property is occupied.

It makes most sense for owners whose homes sit empty for long stretches, because the low season is exactly when occupations go unnoticed past the 48 hour window. Before the quiet months arrive, ask your insurer whether illegal occupation cover is included in your policy or available as an add-on.

irnr_who_pays_en:
Spain taxes your holiday home even if it earns you nothing.

First, the residency test. More than 183 days in Spain in a calendar year, continuous or not, makes you a tax resident. So does having a spouse and underage children living there, or most of your income arising in Spain. Fall outside all of that and you are a non-resident, and IRNR applies. Simply owning triggers it: Spain imputes income at 1.1% of the cadastral value, taxed at 19% for EU and EEA residents and 24% for everyone else. On a €300,000 property, that is around €627 a year at the 19% rate. Selling triggers capital gains tax, usually 19%.

Ignore it and the penalties escalate: fines, closed bank accounts, and in extreme cases property confiscation. Check which side of the 183 days you sat last year, then file Modelo 210 by 31 December.

wealth_tax_en:
Spain has a second tax most owners never meet: wealth tax begins at €700,000.

It applies to residents and non-residents alike. Below €700,000 in assets, nothing is owed. Above it, the tax bites incrementally, only on the value over the line, at progressive rates running from 0.2% to 2.5%. Where you own matters as much as what you own: the tax is shaped by local government, and Madrid applies a 100% discount, taking the bill there to zero. Residents also get an extra €300,000 allowance on a main home they live in.

Who does it catch? Non-residents with a high value Spanish property, or several assets in the country that quietly add up past the threshold. Total your Spanish assets once a year. If you are anywhere near the line, get advice for your specific region, because geography changes everything.

modelo210_scenarios_en:
Bought in June? Sold in March? Modelo 210 does not charge you for a full year.

The imputed tax prorates by days of ownership. The formula: cadastral value x 2% (or 1.1% where the municipality has had a general cadastral revision in the last 10 years) x 19% for EU and EEA residents or 24% for everyone else, x days owned over 365. A UK owner with a cadastral value of €45,986 pays about €220 for a full year. Buy mid-year and your first return is due the following year, covering only your days of ownership. Sell and you file for the days up to completion, early the next year.

Rent for part of the year and there are two pieces: rental income declared annually, plus imputed tax for the days the property stood empty. Co-owners each file and pay their own share. Find your cadastral value on your IBI bill and run the numbers.

spanish_wills_en:
Die in Spain without the right paperwork and Spanish law, not you, decides who inherits.

Spain runs on forced heirship, the Law of Obligatory Heirs. Half of the joint property goes to your spouse. The rest is split into thirds: one third divided equally between your children, one third shared among the children as you choose, and only the final third freely yours to leave to anyone at all. Make no will and a strict order applies instead: children first, natural and adopted, then parents, then the surviving spouse, then wider relatives, and finally the state itself.

That leaves no room for stepchildren, unmarried partners or friends unless a will names them, which matters enormously for anyone who has remarried. Some autonomous regions apply their own variations too. If your family does not fit Spain's default, make a Spanish will or state your wishes clearly in an international one.

inheritance_tax_en:
In Spain, heirs pay the tax before they touch the inheritance.

Succession tax falls on the beneficiary, not the estate, and the estate is not released until the bill is paid. Rates are progressive, from 7.65% to 36.5%, and they vary sharply by region: Andalucia sits among the lowest in the country. The relationship between the deceased and the beneficiary, and the value inherited, also shape the final figure. Residents and non-residents alike pay it on assets located in Spain.

The deadline is 6 months, though an extension is possible. Miss it and 5% is added every 3 months, up to a maximum of 20% on top. One reach worth knowing: assets outside Spain escape Spanish inheritance tax unless the beneficiary is a Spanish resident. If you stand to inherit Spanish property, start the paperwork early. Six months disappears fast across two legal systems.

inheritance_foreign_law_en:
One clause in your will decides whether Spanish forced heirship applies to everything you own.

Under the European Inheritance Regulation of 2012, anyone who dies after 17 August 2015 can choose the inheritance law of their home country instead of the law of their country of residence. The mechanism has one strict condition: the choice must be stated clearly in a Spanish or international will. Live in Spain and stay silent, and Spanish law governs your entire estate, including the forced shares reserved for spouse and children.

It reaches non-residents too. If you keep a holiday home in Spain, your will should state which country's law governs those Spanish assets, or the default can still catch them. So reread your existing will. If it predates your Spanish property and names no governing law, amend it while the choice is still yours to make.

gift_tax_en:
Gift a property or a sum of money in Spain and the recipient has 30 days to pay tax on it.

Gift tax here falls on the person receiving, not the person giving. If you are planning to pass on money or an asset to family, they are the ones who will face the bill, and the clock is short: payment is due within 30 days of the gift being made. Compare that with inheritance tax, where beneficiaries usually get 6 months and can even request an extension. Gifts get no such grace.

The rates are not national either. Gift tax varies from region to region across Spain, so an identical gift can produce a very different bill depending on where the assets and the people involved are. Before transferring anything of value, speak to an adviser who knows your specific region. Timing and geography decide most of the cost.

accountant_worth_en:
No law in Spain says a property buyer needs an accountant. The NIE is mandatory, the notary is mandatory, the accountant is not.

Where one earns the fee: knowing that 6 to 10% lands on top of the asking price as VAT on a new build or transfer tax on a resale. Knowing that the 10% deposit at the Contrato de Arras often goes straight to the seller, and that a safeguarded account is the safer route. Spotting the increasingly sophisticated scams aimed at foreign buyers. Catching the small tax law changes that non-residents rarely notice until they become a problem.

The honest trade-off: a recommended accountant who speaks your language costs real money, especially long term, and hidden fees exist in this industry too. Simple purchase, comfortable with deadlines? You may not need one. Distance, complexity or rental plans? It usually repays itself. Either way, get full costs in writing first.

tax_installments_en:
In Spain, a late tax bill gets cheaper the faster you move. And if you cannot pay it all, there is a plan for that.

File voluntarily before the tax office contacts you, a Declaracion Extemporanea sin Requerimiento Previo, and the penalty shrinks to a surcharge: 1% plus 1% for each month late, rising to 15% plus interest once you pass 12 months. The moment a formal notice arrives, that discounted route closes. If the bill itself is the problem, the Agencia Tributaria accepts installment plans. You justify the hardship, unemployment for example, larger sums may need a guarantee, and interest keeps running. Not perfect, but far better than an accumulating tax debt.

Made an error rather than missed a deadline? A Declaracion Complementaria corrects it, ideally before any letter lands. If you know you are late, file this week, not after the notice.

ibi_deep_en:
IBI is the Spanish tax that stays with the house, even when the owner changes.

The bill is your property's cadastral value, an official valuation from the Land Registry based on location, size, age and characteristics, usually below market value, multiplied by your municipality's rate. Across Spain that averages 0.3% to 1.1%. Santander, Zaragoza and Madrid sit low; parts of Catalunya and the Costa Blanca run higher. Bills arrive between May and October, and many councils will not post abroad, so electronic notification matters.

Ignore it and the sequence is predictable: a reminder, then surcharges from around 5% rising to 20% or more, then debt collection, meaning money seized from your Spanish account, charges placed against the property and trouble when you try to sell. Unpaid IBI can stay attached to the property, so buyers should check before purchase. Set up a direct debit and request electronic notices from the town hall.

bank_fees_en:
A Spanish current account can charge you in five different ways before you notice one.

The headline cost is the maintenance fee, billed monthly, quarterly or once a year. Around it sit the quieter ones: a fee simply for holding a credit or debit card, spending requirements where missing a minimum number of transactions or a minimum spend triggers a penalty, withdrawal fees at ATMs outside your bank's network, and transfer fees that climb when money crosses borders. On average, Spanish bank fees run higher than in much of Europe.

Which account you need matters too. Living in Spain means a resident account for daily use. Owning property while living abroad usually points to a non-resident account. Before opening either, ask for the complete fee schedule in writing and confirm exactly which ATMs count as in-network.

free_banking_myth_en:
Free banking in Spain usually means an account that is free only while you behave exactly as the bank hopes.

Several major banks charge around €240 a year in maintenance on a standard current account. A credit card adds roughly €20, a debit card up to 30. Miss the minimum monthly card spend or transaction count and extra fees start stacking. Take out a mortgage and you may be required to hold the bank's property insurance for at least the first year.

International transfers are the quiet drain. Moving money from another currency can cost up to €35 per transfer, so a pension arriving every month can lose hundreds a year to fees alone. Before signing, map your real usage, monthly card spend and transfers in and out, and check it line by line against the account's conditions.

credit_card_fees_en:
A perfect credit score at home is worth nothing to a Spanish bank.

Credit history stays in the country where you built it. If you spend fewer than 180 days a year in Spain, have no income there and no spouse or child living there, a Spanish credit card is unlikely to be offered at all. The main exception is when holding a card for a minimum period is written into your mortgage conditions. Residents rebuild their record slowly, and putting utilities in your name is one of the fastest ways to do it.

The fees have their own logic. Annual card fees and minimum spend rules sometimes only begin after the first year. Foreign transaction fees apply when your Spanish card pays in another currency. And if a terminal offers to charge your foreign card in pounds, that is dynamic currency conversion: convenient, but the rate and fees run high. Choose euros.

cash_rules_en:
Withdrawing €3,000 in Spain now means telling the tax office a day in advance.

Under rules in force since 2025, withdrawals above €3,000, or any amount involving €500 notes, must be reported to the tax agency 24 hours ahead. You notify via its website with proof of ID, sometimes proof of where the funds came from, and receive a certificate to present at the bank. From €100,000 the notice period is 72 hours.

Cash payments have their own caps: €1,000 for transactions involving a business or between private individuals, 10,000 for non-residents not taxed in Spain. Fines run from 50 to 150 percent of the amount, though self-reporting within three months may earn an exemption. Travellers must declare over €10,000 at the border. Keep receipts for large transactions for at least five years.

currency_transfer_en:
In a Spanish property purchase, the deadline is fixed and the exchange rate is not.

Once the arras contract is signed, completion funds must land in the right account on time. Arrive late and the 10 percent deposit can be lost. That makes the transfer plan part of the purchase itself, not an afterthought. Exchange rates move throughout the day, so rather than guessing, set rate alerts and transfer when the level works in your favour. On a purchase-sized sum, a small difference in rate is real money.

Check three things about any provider before sending anything: that client funds are held in segregated accounts, separate from the business's own money, that fees are stated upfront rather than folded into the rate, and that regular payments, a pension or a mortgage abroad, can be automated and tracked. Plan the transfer timeline the day you sign the arras.

nie_realities_en:
Most NIE applications stall before anyone reaches the police station.

The process runs in a strict order. First comes the modelo 790 payment form, and here is the catch: the fee usually cannot be paid online or by card. You take the form to a bank branch, pay there, and keep the proof of payment, because the police station will ask for it. Only then does the appointment make sense.

The application itself is the EX-18 form, in two copies, submitted in Spanish; the English version is a guide, not a valid submission. You also need a translated letter explaining why you need the number, such as a purchase or mortgage agreement, a passport with at least a year of validity, photocopies and photos. Requirements shift between regions, and you can apply through the Spanish embassy at home or via a lawyer instead. Check your own municipality's list first.

lost_documents_en:
Every lost Spanish property document has a specific route back.

Deeds are the easiest once you know where to look. The notary who executed your escritura or title deed holds the original and issues certified copies, usually between 20 and €100. Forgotten which notary it was? The Land Registry where the property is registered can tell you. The Nota Simple, the registry extract listing owner, debts and legal status, is reordered online for around €10, and costs more in person through the registrars.

A stolen NIE starts at the police: file a denuncia, then request a duplicate with the EX-15 form and the Tasa 790 payment. An energy certificate comes from the technician who issued it, or a new assessor for 60 to €150, and notaries may refuse to complete a sale without one. Scan every document today, before you need any of this.

local_tax_office_en:
The tax office that matters most to homeowners is not the national one.

Every municipality runs an Oficina de Recaudación Municipal, collecting local taxes for the town hall, entirely separate from the national agency that handles income tax. In some provinces the work passes to a provincial collection agency. This office bills your IBI, calculated on the property's cadastral value rather than its market value, plus the waste tax and vehicle tax.

The waste tax surprises absent owners: 50 to €200 a year, usually billed between June and October, owed even if you never visit, and some councils base it on water use or bin count. Vehicle tax follows fiscal horsepower and emissions, from about €20 to over 200, often due on January 1. Bills arrive by post or sit unseen on the office's online portal, which is exactly how absent owners miss them. Set up direct debits for all three.

utilities_setup_en:
In Spain you can choose your electricity supplier, sometimes your gas supplier, and never your water company.

Water is fixed to the building, run by the municipality or an assigned private operator. Changing it into your name means going to the town hall to register the change of ownership and sign a new contract. If the property is not connected at all, expect a much longer process, so start early. Gas is on the mains only in certain towns; elsewhere canisters are the norm, and gas appliances need a yearly safety check costing around €70.

Signing up for any supply takes ID, your NIE, Spanish bank account details and proof of address, after which a technician connects the property. Inheriting the previous owner's contracts? Confirm every past bill is paid before signing. The moment the arras contract is signed is the moment to start comparing providers.

healthcare_access_en:
Public healthcare in Spain is reached through one of four doors.

Door one is work: employed or self-employed, your social security contributions register you with the national system. Door two is the S1 form, for those whose home government pays for their care, typically state pensioners, and cover extends to dependents such as spouses and children. Door three is time: after five years in Spain you can apply for permanent residency and gain the same access as a national. Door four, for non-workers resident over a year, is the Convenio Especial, a pay-in scheme with monthly contributions.

UK nationals visiting use an EHIC while valid, then a GHIC, and need proof of healthcare coverage before a visa or residency. Once inside the system, the state pays 40 to 60 percent of prescription costs, retirees pay just 10, and only emergency dental is covered. Work out which door is yours before you move.

consorcio_insurance_en:
Spain quietly insures every policyholder against earthquakes and floods, and most owners never notice.

A mandatory surcharge on ordinary insurance policies funds a state-backed scheme, the Consorcio de Compensación de Seguros, which pays out for extraordinary risks: flooding, wave battering, winds above 120 km/h, tornados, earthquakes, tsunamis, volcanic eruptions, even falling meteorites. Slower winds, landslides, subsidence and avalanches stay with your private insurer, and gaps like hail, frost or lightning can be added as optional covers.

Claims are simpler than people expect. Cover is automatic, no official disaster declaration is required, and there is no upper or lower limit. Document the damage safely, photograph everything, then claim directly with the scheme or through your insurer. Flooding accounts for around 70 percent of its payouts. Check your policy today and confirm the extraordinary risk surcharge is on it.

uk_move_en:
The S1 form only works if you request it before leaving the UK.

That is the pattern of this move: the critical steps happen in the wrong-looking order. Pensioners request the S1 from the UK government before departure, because it is what lets Spain register them for public healthcare. Proof of healthcare coverage comes before the visa or residency application, not after. Students need proof of enrollment to access the social security system. And your passport anchors both the NIE, the foreigner's number used for buying property, banking and utilities, and the TIE, the physical card that carries it.

Belongings are the one place to slow down. Use an accredited remover experienced with UK to Europe moves, or skip shipping altogether, since furniture in Spain is often cheaper than transporting your own. Sequence healthcare, visa and NIE before booking the removal van.

contract_glossary_en:
A Spanish property purchase is not one contract. It is a sequence, and each document binds you differently.

It starts with the offer contract at the agency: around €2,000 secures your bid, refunded if the seller declines, or credited toward agency fees of 3 to 5 percent. Next comes the arras, the first document that legally binds both sides, with completion usually set 2 to 3 months out. Make sure that window fits your paperwork and any mortgage.

With a mortgage, you sign a FEIN before the deed. Without one, a Contrato de Compraventa is drawn up instead, sometimes by the agency itself, fixing the price and the seller's obligation to sell. The escritura publica at the notary closes the sequence. Map the whole chain before you sign the first link.

escritura_notary_en:
The notary is not your lawyer. In Spain, the notary is impartial by design.

At the escritura publica, the deed of sale, the notary prepares and oversees the document, reads it out to buyer and seller together and checks both fully understand it before anyone signs. If your Spanish is not strong, you may be required to bring a translator or a Spanish speaking legal adviser. With a mortgage, you meet the notary at least 24 hours before signing the mortgage deed so they can take you through the loan conditions first.

What the notary does not do is represent your interests. They act as an impartial adviser to both parties and confirm the sale is legal. And signing is not the finish line: the property and the new owners still have to be registered at the Land Registry Office afterwards. Bring your own adviser and plan that step.

arras_contract_en:
The arras contract decides what you actually bought. Most buyers only check the price.

Beyond price and an accurate description, the contract must fix the completion date, the penalties if either side pulls out, and the specifics: furniture the sellers leave, repairs they agreed to pay for, whether appliances are included, whether water and electricity will be switched on. If it is not written in the arras, it was never agreed.

You receive the draft a couple of days before the agreed signing date. That window exists so you or your representative can request amendments, so use it. When the 10 percent is paid, it often goes directly to the owners; common, but a safeguarded account at a financial institution is the safer route. Buying new build, add completion date clauses too. Read the draft the day it arrives, not at the table.

land_registry_en:
The Spanish Land Registry will show a property's history to anyone with a legitimate interest. That includes you, before you buy.

The Registro de la Propiedad is a public register supervised by the Ministry of Justice. Prospective buyers, lawyers, heirs and administrators can all access it. It records size, address, use, every ownership change and any debts attached. That is how you confirm a seller really owns what they are selling; there have been cases of squatters selling homes that were never theirs.

Knowing your office matters too. Rural areas may have a single Land Registry Office, while Valencia has 18 and Alicante 8; the first line of your Nota Simple names the one responsible. And after signing at the notary, registration is a separate step. Only once registered are you officially recognised as owner, so register promptly after completion.

bank_guarantee_en:
Off plan in Spain can mean paying up to 80 percent of the price before the home exists. One document protects that money.

Since Law 57/68, developers taking staged payments must do two things. First, open a specific bank account for buyer deposits, not a personal or previously held one, usable only for the construction of the property. Second, provide a bank guarantee that refunds every payment plus interest if the build is not started or not finished by the agreed completion date. The guarantee must have no expiry date; it stays valid until the property is fully finished and safe to live in.

It costs you nothing. It costs the developer a lot, which is why some try to work around it, sometimes by offering better conditions instead. If a developer resists the guarantee, walk away, whatever the discount.

rural_property_en:
Rural land in Spain fails checks that urban flats pass. Run these before you fall for the finca.

First, compare paper to ground. The Land Registry and the Cadastral Registry frequently disagree with real life on plot size, property description and boundaries, and any discrepancy brings legal and financial consequences. If the Title Deed is missing or outdated, wait until the vendor updates it at the Land Registry, at their expense, before proceeding. Rural plots also carry easements urban homes rarely do: rights of way, of view, to extract water.

Then check the build is legal. Some owners register a casa de aperos, a shed, to dodge planning rules and build a villa; a surveyor can confirm Town Hall permission, and without it you should walk away. Pre 1956 constructions are usually legal but often cannot be extended. Finally, wastewater: septic tanks are the norm, and a renovation can force a modern replacement costing thousands. Hire an independent surveyor before signing anything.

leasehold_freehold_en:
In Spain, freehold is the default. But leasehold exists, and the contract will not use that English word.

Watch for derecho de uso, usufructo or concesion administrativa. These mean you hold the right to use the property for a set period, usually 30 to 99 years, after which rights revert to the freeholder. You do not own the land underneath and, in most Spanish leasehold cases, not the property either. It appears in commercial space, government owned land, historic buildings and timeshare developments.

Financing and resale follow the clock. Spanish banks prefer freehold; a leasehold mortgage generally requires 60 to 75 years remaining, a high demand location and a strong financial profile, and still comes with smaller loans and stricter terms. Value can fall as the term shortens, since buyers fear their time will be cut short. The Nota Simple confirms whether a property is freehold or leasehold, so request it before signing any arras.

buying_cost_stages_en:
You do not pay for a Spanish property once. You pay in three stages, and a few bills hide after completion.

Stage one is the reservation fee, usually 1,000 to €6,000, paid to secure your bid while the arras contract is drawn up. If the deal falls through in that window, it is returned; if the purchase goes ahead, it is refunded or taken off the price. Stage two: 10 percent of the purchase sum at the arras, reservation fee included, ideally into a safeguarded account. Stage three: the remaining 90 percent when you sign the deed at the notary.

Then the forgotten lines. Registering the property is the buyer's responsibility and generally costs 500 to €1,000. Notary fees run from 0.01 to 2 percent of the price. And every owner pays a rubbish collection fee 1 to 4 times a year by direct debit. Budget the stages first, then the small print.

new_build_vs_resale_en:
New build or pre owned in Spain? The wrong question is which looks nicer. The right one is what becomes your problem at signing.

With a pre owned home, hidden defects and illegal renovations transfer with the keys. Once the property is in your name, they are your issues and can be very expensive to resolve. So interrogate the listing: how long has it been on the market, why is the owner selling, has it been renovated before, what do community fees, utilities and insurance cost, are there outstanding debts, and what are the neighbours like.

Taxes differ too. IBI, the annual property tax, is based on the cadastral value and varies by region and by whether the home is a new build, so confirm the figure before you commit. Renovating can add real value, but restrictions apply, so check them first if renovation is the plan. Have an expert inspect before any offer.

property_search_en:
Most buyers start with property portals. The paperwork should start months earlier.

The order matters. You need a NIE, the foreigner identity number, to make an offer at all, and appointment queues can be long, so apply early; go in person to the police station or foreigner's office and you leave with it the same day. Non EU citizens should also check the visa position: 90 days in any 180 without a residence permit.

Budget before browsing. Experts recommend at least 10 percent on top of the price for notary, purchase taxes, land registry and legal costs, and purchase tax rates vary by region; on the Costa Blanca it is 10 percent. Then assemble the people: an agent with non public listings, ideally SIRA affiliated, and a lawyer, who can even hold power of attorney and act while you are abroad. Sort this sequence first; viewings come last.

brexit_buying_en:
Brexit did not change the price of a Spanish home by one euro. It changed almost everything around it.

The right to buy never depended on nationality, and purchase costs, tax, notary and registration fees are identical for UK and EU buyers. What changed sits downstream. Non resident income tax on rental income rose from 19 to 24 percent for Brits, and rental expenses can no longer be deducted before the tax is applied, though tax paid in Spain can be offset against tax in the UK.

Logistics tightened too. Mortgages involve more paperwork and can take longer, NIE appointments can be slower for UK applicants, and visits are capped at 90 days in any 180 without a residence permit. The Golden Visa route for larger property investors has also ended. If you plan to rent out or stay long, model the 24 percent and the calendar before you buy.

market_seasons_en:
In the Spanish property market, the calendar is a pricing tool.

Spring is prime selling season. Buyers want to exchange well before the warm weather so they can enjoy the property in time, and homes show at their best with gardens and balconies in bloom. Autumn runs hot too: tourists return home wanting their own slice of Spain, and families push to finalise before the school year, competition that can lift prices in popular coastal towns.

Winter is the buyer's window. Few people make a significant financial decision with Christmas around the corner, so sellers are more willing to negotiate and prices can sit lower than the rest of the year. Two quirks to plan around: in August many agencies, lawyers and banks close for most of the month and deals stall, while local events like the Fallas in Valencia in March or Seville's feria in May create local spikes in interest. Selling, aim for late summer or early autumn; buying, hunt in winter.

tourist_license_en:
A rental contract under three months makes you a tourist landlord in Spain, and that requires a licence.

There are two forms: an individual licence for private owners and a collective one for companies managing several properties. To apply, you prepare the property to hygiene and safety standards, obtain habitability and energy efficiency certificates, register with the local tourism agency where required, then file the application at your tourist office. Approval takes between one and six months depending on region and demand.

Skip it and fines typically run from 4,000 to €60,000, rising sharply for repeat infractions, and reaching €111,000 in Ibiza. Catalunya has dedicated teams tracking illegal lets, Barcelona bans short-term private room rentals, and Valencia mostly issues new licences to ground-floor properties only. Before buying with rental plans, check licence availability in that exact area.

community_rental_ban_en:
Your building can now legally vote your tourist rental out of existence.

Since 2019, Article 17.12 of the Horizontal Property Law has let owner communities condition and limit tourist lets, but judges across Spain disagreed on whether limiting included banning, and the law never defined a voting threshold. The Supreme Court has settled both points: prohibition is a form of limitation, and a three-fifths majority, 60 percent of owners, is enough. No unanimous vote is required.

The case that forced the issue came from Marbella, where owners voted 48 to 3 to ban tourist flats after complaints about noise, damage and misuse of common spaces; two companies owning six apartments lost in court. Two safeguards remain: bans are not retroactive, and they must be properly justified with problems still affecting residents. If you let short term in a community building, check your statutes and attend the next assembly.

noneu_tax_proposal_en:
Spain has proposed a 100 percent tax on property purchases by non-EU buyers.

It targets non-residents, meaning anyone spending under 183 days a year in Spain, which includes UK and US buyers of second homes. It is one of twelve measures announced to tackle a housing crisis in which prices have nearly doubled in a decade and Madrid and Barcelona rents rose by as much as 33 percent in five years. It also lands alongside the Golden Visa closing on April 3rd 2025, ending residency through €500,000 property purchases.

Scale matters here: in 2023, foreigners bought 15 percent of Spanish properties, 87,000 of 583,000 sales, but non-EU non-residents accounted for just 27,000, around 5 percent, mostly coastal holiday homes rather than city flats. For context, Valencia currently charges everyone the same 10 percent transfer tax. This remains a proposal under study with no final text, so watch the legislation before restructuring any purchase plans.

hoa_how_it_works_en:
Buy an apartment in Spain and you automatically join the Comunidad de Propietarios. There is no opt-out.

The community runs under the Ley de Propiedad Horizontal, first enacted in 1960 and updated since. Fees scale with property size, so a penthouse pays more than a ground-floor flat, and most communities collect quarterly with a surplus on top, a buffer that later covers big jobs like repainting the facade every decade or so. A president, elected from the owners or rotated yearly, calls meetings; some communities also hire an external administrator to collect fees by direct debit and organise repairs.

The annual general assembly decides budgets, repairs and house rules, from pool quiet hours to pets. Notice must be at least 3 days, usually two weeks, and proxy voting is allowed. One telling rule: vote against installing a lift and you may avoid paying, but you get no key. Before buying, have a lawyer confirm exactly what you will pay.

hoa_disagree_vote_en:
In a Spanish owners' community, losing a vote is annoying. Ignoring the fees can cost you the property.

Most community decisions pass by majority, and votes are weighted, so one person owning several flats in your building holds a larger share of the outcome. It is worth checking who owns what before you buy. Proxy voting is allowed on important matters. If you disagree with a result, there are only two grounds to have a vote revoked: it is contrary to the law, or it is detrimental to the community. Preference alone changes nothing.

Refusing to pay your share is different territory: it leads to legal action that can end in seizure of the home and its public sale at auction. And because community debts attach to the property, request the Nota Simple before signing the Arras contract; any debt it reveals can be deducted from the selling price. Make that document your first ask.

rental_roi_en:
Coastal Spain peaks in summer. Spanish cities do the opposite, filling up in the cooler months.

That inversion is the starting point for seasonal rental returns. Work out who actually rents in your area: family destinations peak in school holidays, while digital nomads often prefer the low season and will pay for a proper work area. Before any of this, confirm tourist licence availability where you are buying; popular cities barely issue new ones, and Barcelona plans to revoke licences it already granted.

The levers that raise returns are unglamorous: dynamic pricing that moves with demand, discounts for extended stays, and early-booking promotions that double as repeat-visit incentives. Positive reviews drive visibility and future bookings. Buy durable furniture rather than cheap pieces that fail fast, and treat community improvements like lifts or extra parking as value adds, not just costs. Fix small faults before they become expensive ones, then price each season deliberately.

pest_prevention_en:
A Spanish holiday home left empty for months is a pantry moth's favourite address.

Spain's climate breeds a different cast of pests than northern Europe: cockroaches, some of which fly, plus ants, mosquitoes in humid or leafy areas, fruit flies, rats in roofs and gardens, and pantry moths that can force you to bin your entire dry food store. Heat spoils everything faster, which is why Spanish street bins are emptied so often. So before you fly home, empty the cupboards of flour, pasta, grains and tea, and take the rubbish out.

Block the routes in: fit window nets and screen doors, seal cracks at the back of cupboards, put the plug in drains overnight and pour boiling water down them regularly, because cockroaches will use pipes. Know the warning signs too: hissing behind cupboards, scuttling overhead, droppings, gnaw marks, or pets fixating on one spot. Bay leaves in cupboards deter moths and roaches; for serious cases, pest firms work discreetly with unmarked vans. Clear the dry goods before every departure.

maintenance_calendar_en:
The Spanish sun is quietly invoicing your roof.

UV exposure makes terracotta tiles brittle and cracks paintwork, while sea air pushes salt into metal fixtures until they corrode, and coastal humidity feeds mould and wood rot. Inland, some villages get snow and ice, and the swing between freezing winters and scorching summers stresses a house further. Hard water zones like Valencia, the Costa Blanca and the Costa del Sol add limescale that shortens the life of pipes and appliances, which is why a water softener earns its keep there.

The defence is a calendar, not a crisis fund. Spring: clear gutters of winter sludge, check the facade for moisture damage, repaint or reseal with UV-resistant paint, and clean the air conditioning before summer. Summer: check outdoor pipes and irrigation. Autumn: inspect the roof for sun damage, clean gutters before heavier rain, service the boiler, and test alarms before leaving for long periods. A neglected pool alone can mean an expensive drain and deep clean. Book the autumn round now.

renovation_permits_en:
In Spain you do not get one renovation permit. You need one for each aspect of the work.

Permits come from the city council, the Ayuntamiento, and the legal viability of your plans should be confirmed before you even buy the property. Renovation companies will sometimes handle the permit process for you, though often as a paid extra, so establish who is responsible from day one.

On money, assume the budget will be exceeded however carefully you plan: material prices shift, and old pipes or rotting floorboards surface once walls open. Set a reserve aside for exactly that. Then interrogate any building company before signing: do prices include IVA, are they fixed or variable, does the firm carry third-party insurance, do they complete all work themselves or subcontract specific jobs, and how is material quality assured? Vet them through word of mouth and ask to see a finished project. Greener choices like insulation and solar also lift resale value. Get every answer in writing before work starts.

extension_deeds_en:
That pool, extra floor or enclosed porch is legally an extension in Spain, and it belongs on your deeds.

Structural work needs an Obra Mayor licence; even non-structural jobs like retiling, repainting or same-size window swaps need the Obra Menor. A licensed technical architect drafts the plans, you file them at the town hall, and if the property shares communal spaces your neighbours must approve, with the community's certificate signed before a notary. Expect ICIO tax of 2 to 5 percent of construction cost plus a smaller urban development licence fee, and processing from a few weeks to several months.

When work finishes, the architect issues the Certificado Final de Obra and the extension is declared before a notary and entered in the land registry. Built without a licence? The antiquity certificate can legalise it retrospectively, but works completed after August 2014 must be 15 years old, versus 4 for earlier ones. Unregistered extensions stall sales and risk demolition orders, so legalise before you list.

invest_locations_en:
Coastal rentals sleep in winter. Madrid does not.

That is the sharpest divide in the Spanish market. As the country's political and business hub, Madrid draws a constant flow of professionals, students and international workers, giving year-round rental demand that coastal properties cannot always guarantee, and the metro makes cheaper outskirts genuinely viable. Barcelona still offers Mediterranean city life, but strict Catalan regulation means new tourist licences have stopped, so investors there should plan around long-term tenants, not holidaymakers.

The value stories sit further down the coast. Valencia, Spain's third largest city, combines urban seaside living with more space for your money. Malaga has evolved from tourist gateway into a business hub pulling in remote workers and international companies. Alicante is the overlooked mid-size option with affordable outskirts and good transport, while the Costa Brava's licence restrictions push owners toward mid or long-term lets. Seville is authentic but beachless with very hot summers. Whatever the location, verify its short-term rental rules before you offer.

costa_blanca_en:
The Costa Blanca is 200 kilometres of coastline, and its towns are not interchangeable.

The strip runs from Denia in the north to Pilar de la Horadada in the south, with Alicante and its daily European flights in the middle and around 330 days of sun a year. In the north, Denia pairs a ferry port serving the Balearics with a castle and a strong expat community; Javea splits into port, beach and old town, each with its own property style, and suits active buyers with its sports and watersports scene. Moraira mixes beachfront villas with hillside homes, while Calpe is the bigger everyday town with daily street markets.

Different budgets and temperaments fit different spots: Benissa sits slightly back from the coast with sea views, Altea trades on white lanes and its marina, Torrevieja in the south draws retirees and families near two salt-lake nature parks, and inland Xalo offers vineyard views about thirty minutes from the beach. Match the town's character to how you will actually use the home.

retire_city_town_en:
Retiring to Spain forces one honest choice: city or small town.

Cities win on logistics. Airports, hospitals, cultural life and more property choice sit close by, and urban life barely dips outside summer. The price is literal and social: property generally costs more, homes are smaller, community can be harder to find, and reaching real countryside usually means a car journey. Madrid, Barcelona, Malaga, San Sebastian and Zaragoza rank among the most expensive places to live.

Small towns flip every one of those points. Your money buys a bigger home, possibly with garden and pool, and neighbours actually get to know you. But deeper medical care means travelling to a larger city, remote towns have little or no public transport so a vehicle is essential, and coastal or island towns can empty out in winter, with shops and restaurants closing for the season. In some villages, Catalan or Basque may be the daily language. A larger town near a big city is the classic compromise. Whatever you shortlist, visit in low season first.

modelo210_en:
Own a home in Spain that stands empty most of the year? Spain still expects a tax return for it.
Modelo 210 applies to every non-resident owner, even when the property earns nothing. The tax is built on the cadastral value from your IBI bill, not the market price: that value times 1.1% or 2%, then taxed at 19% for EU and EEA residents or 24% for everyone else, including the UK. The return for an empty home is due by 31 December of the following year, and each co-owner files separately for their share.
If you rent the home out, that income is declared annually as well, and booking platforms now report your revenue to the Spanish tax office, so the figures need to match. Unfiled years usually surface when you sell. Set a calendar reminder for early December and file before anyone has to ask.

buying_fees_en:
The asking price is never the real price in Spain.
Plan for 12-14% on top before you fall in love with a listing. On resales the biggest piece is transfer tax, which varies by region, so the same home can cost thousands more a few kilometres away. New builds pay 10% VAT instead, plus stamp duty. Then come the fixed costs: notary fees of roughly €1,000 on a €250,000 purchase, land registry fees of 400-€700, and a lawyer at a few thousand euros or a gestor at a few hundred.
Borrowing adds its own layer, with bank setup fees of up to 2% of the loan and valuation reports of 250-€600 that sometimes land on the buyer. All of it falls due around completion, so keep that money liquid, not invested. Ask for a full written cost breakdown before you sign anything.

scams_en:
If a Spanish property deal feels rushed, that is the biggest red flag of all.
Pressure is the scammer's main tool, because every real check takes a little time. Before any money moves, order a Nota Simple from the Land Registry and confirm that the person selling is actually the registered owner. If the names do not match, stop and ask why. And if payment details suddenly change by email just before a deposit is due, treat it as a hijacked conversation: call the agency on the number from their official website, never the one in the message.
Renting instead of buying? Ask for the tourist licence number and look it up in the regional registry yourself rather than taking a screenshot on trust. Make it a rule that no transfer leaves your account until every detail has been verified in writing. Honest sellers never mind the extra day.

owners_year_en:
Spanish property bills do not arrive all at once. They arrive all year.
IBI, the local property tax, is charged to whoever owns the home at the start of the year, and the bill lands between May and October depending on the municipality. It often goes only to a Spanish address, which is how absent owners miss it. The simplest fix is a direct debit with the town hall, so the bill gets paid whether you are there or not.
Community fees tick along monthly or quarterly, with any increases decided at the annual general meeting. The non-resident tax return then closes the year on 31 December. Put all three on one annual calendar, set up direct debits for the recurring ones, and have someone check the mailbox. Most surprises are really just missed post.

nie_application_en:
You cannot buy a home in Spain without one small piece of paper.
The NIE number itself never expires, but for a property purchase the certificate is usually only accepted for three months, so time the application to your buying window. The fee is paid at a bank branch first, using form 790, and you bring the stamped proof to the appointment along with two copies of the application form, your passport, photocopies, passport photos and a letter explaining why you need the number.
Queues at the police station can close around 13:30, so arrive early, and in busy areas the online appointments are booked out weeks ahead. Non-EU citizens, including Brits, should start well before the property search, since their waits run longer, and you can also apply through the Spanish consulate at home. Book the appointment before you book the viewing trip.

sepa_swift_en:
Sending money to Spain the wrong way costs you at every step.
SWIFT transfers travel through correspondent banks, and each intermediary in the chain can take its own fee before the money lands. SEPA was built to fix exactly that: it covers euro payments across the EU, EEA and the UK, needs nothing more than an IBAN, and moves money quickly at little or no cost. Most UK banks already send euro transfers as SEPA by default, but confirm it before a large payment.
One catch remains. Spain runs its own domestic network for direct debits, and many utilities and town halls will only collect from a Spanish account, so a local account still earns its keep. Send euros, not your home currency, let SEPA carry them, and keep the Spanish account for the bills.

community_fees_en:
Community fees are the running cost new owners underestimate most.
They fund lifts, pools, gardens, security and the fabric of the building itself, and the range is wide: some owners pay around €100 a quarter while high-end developments can run past 1,000. Your share depends on the services provided and the size of your property, which also sets your voting weight at the annual general meeting where budgets and increases are decided.
Two protections matter before you buy. Ask for a certificate confirming the seller owes nothing, because part of any old debt can pass to you with the keys. And know that unpaid fees carry real consequences, from interest and legal costs to, in extreme cases, a forced sale. Once you own, attend the meeting or send a proxy. That is where fee rises and big works are decided.

solar_energy_en:
Solar panels in Spain pay for themselves faster than most people expect.
With more than 300 sunny days a year, most homes see electricity bills fall by 30-80%, and the sun tax that once made panels pointless was abolished back in 2019. A typical installation costs 6,000-€10,000 depending on the property and system, and some tariffs let you sell surplus power back to the grid. South-facing roofs produce the most, so have the installer assess orientation before quoting.
Two details surprise owners. Without a battery, a grid-tied system shuts off during a power cut for safety, so blackout protection costs extra. And demand is now so high in some areas that waiting lists run to months. Ask your town hall about IBI discounts for solar homes before you commit. The savings stack up quietly.

holiday_home_cost_en:
What does a holiday home in Spain cost in the months you are not there?
For a typical 50-100 m2 apartment, the baseline runs to roughly €333 a month once you add community fees, electricity, water, gas, internet, insurance, IBI and the non-resident tax. Add key holding or a management company at 50-€100 and an alarm at around 50, and 400-€500 a month is realistic. A villa often costs double or more: electricity alone can hit 300-€500 in summer with the air conditioning running, and a pool pushes the water bill up.
The useful trick is to budget yearly rather than monthly, because IBI and insurance arrive as single large bills instead of tidy instalments. Keep a buffer in the account for exactly those months. An empty home still works quietly through your account.

buying_10_steps_en:
The arras contract is the moment a Spanish purchase turns serious.
Walk away after signing and you lose your 10% deposit. If the seller walks, they owe you double. That symmetry is why the arras matters more than the offer itself. You receive the contract a couple of days before signing, so read it with your lawyer, and pay the deposit into a safeguarded account rather than straight to the seller, even though direct payment is common in Spain.
The arras also fixes the completion date, often around two months out, which is your window to finalise the mortgage. Once you accept the bank's offer, the FEIN starts a mandatory 10-day reflection period before the deeds can be signed, so build it into the timeline. Order the Nota Simple and finish every legal check before you sign the arras, never after.

nota_simple_en:
The cheapest document in a Spanish property purchase can save you the most money.
A Nota Simple from the Land Registry shows the registered owner, mortgages, embargoes and unpaid debts, plus boundaries, square metres and the land classification. In Spain those debts travel with the home, not the seller, so this one page tells you what you would really be buying. It also lists the cadastral value, which a bank may look at when sizing your mortgage.
Anyone with a legitimate interest can order one, around €10 online and a little more in person, and the online copy usually arrives the same day. You will need the property details or its registry identifier, which your agent can supply. Order one before the arras contract, then order a fresh copy right before signing. Things can change between viewing and completion.

plusvalia_en:
Buying from a non-resident seller in Spain quietly changes who pays what.
Two duties shift onto the buyer. First, you withhold 3% of the purchase price and pay it to the tax office within a month, as an advance on the seller's capital gains bill; if the final tax comes to less, the seller claims the difference back. Second, plusvalia, the municipal tax on the rise in urban land value, is filed by you when the seller lives abroad, paid from money withheld from the seller, with 30 days for it to reach the council.
The plusvalia amount depends on local rates and how long the seller owned the home, up to a 20-year cap, and if the land value genuinely fell there may be nothing to pay. Agree in writing before completion who handles each payment and which sums are withheld. It saves arguments later.

rental_rule_changes_en:
Renting out your Spanish home short term? The rules changed in 2025.
Every rental property now needs its own registration number from a single national register, and the number must appear on the advert. Platforms are required to check it and are removing listings without one. Registration runs through the Colegio de Registradores and asks for proof of ownership and proof that you comply with local and regional rules, and the code is only issued if your building allows tourist lets.
The number stays valid for 12 months. Renewal means listing the leases from the past year and, for short lets, signing a declaracion responsable explaining why they were short term. Two actions follow: read your community statutes, because a vote to ban tourist rentals binds you, and set a renewal reminder before the code lapses.

epc_certificates_en:
You can be fined for a Spanish property advert before anyone even views the home.
The energy certificate is required at the advertising stage, not just at the sale, and advertising without one typically draws fines of 300-€600, rising to 1,000-6,000 for providing no certificate at all or falsifying one. Getting one is simple: a certified technician inspects insulation, windows, heating, cooling and lighting, then issues a rating from A to G. Expect 100-€300 and less than a week.
The certificate stays valid for ten years, and a decent rating can support your asking price and open access to green subsidies. One step is easily missed: the certificate must be registered with your regional authority, and an unregistered one does not count. Confirm the technician files it, and keep the reference with your property papers.

buyer_visas_en:
Buying a home in Spain no longer buys you the right to stay.
The golden visa is closed to new applicants, so a purchase and a residence permit are now two entirely separate questions. The non-lucrative visa is the classic route for retirees and other non-workers: it asks for passive income of about €28,000 a year and does not allow you to work. The digital nomad visa suits remote workers earning around €2,500 a month for a foreign employer or clients.
No visa at all? The 90/180 rule still gives generous part-time use: up to 90 days in any rolling 180, counted across the whole Schengen area, not per country. Applications for the visa routes start at the Spanish consulate in your home country, before you move. Decide which path fits your life, then count your days carefully.

citizenship_en:
Marrying a Spaniard does not hand you a Spanish passport.
The standard route to citizenship is ten years of continuous legal residence in Spain. Marriage shortens that to one year, but only if you actually live in the country as a legal resident for that year; a marriage certificate alone changes nothing. Residence also has to be continuous, so long stretches spent abroad can undermine the application.
Everyone sits the same two exams: the CCSE test on Spanish culture and society, and the DELE A2 language exam, both passed before you apply. Then comes the question many discover too late: dual citizenship. For many nationalities, taking the Spanish passport means formally giving up the old one, while some countries are exempt. Check your own country's rules before you start the process, not after.

retiring_spain_en:
Retiring to Spain costs less than many expect. The paperwork decides everything else.
Spend more than 183 days a year in the country and you become tax resident, with worldwide income, pensions included, taxed in Spain at progressive rates. Double tax treaties usually stop the same income being taxed twice, but the filing still has to happen. Larger estates should note the wealth tax on net assets above €700,000, softened by a €300,000 allowance on your main home and waived entirely in some regions.
The visa route asks for proof of funds and private health cover without co-payments, with policies for retirees commonly running 50-€200 a month until you qualify for the public system. Outside the big cities, 18,000-€27,000 a year buys a comfortable life. Choose your region first, then count your days.

property_insurance_en:
Home insurance is not legally required in Spain. Skipping it is still a bad idea.
If you have a mortgage, the bank will insist on cover anyway, and the policy it sells can cost well above market price, so you are free to buy elsewhere even if the bank nudges your interest rate in return. Know the difference between building cover and contents cover, check that liability is included, and see what your community's block policy already insures so you do not pay twice for the same walls.
Holiday homes need one extra question answered. Many standard policies limit payouts if the property sits empty for months, and a burst pipe that goes unnoticed is exactly the claim that gets refused. If you rent out, look at cover for tenant damage too. Ask specifically about vacant-home cover before you sign.

direct_debit_en:
In Spain, the company decides when your bill leaves your account. Not you.
Direct debits run on a signed SEPA mandate carrying your IBAN, the amount, the frequency and a start date, and each provider then picks its own collection day. For many recurring bills, utilities included, direct debit is effectively the only payment method on offer, which is why the mandate matters more than it seems.
Switching banks is where it stings. Nothing transfers automatically: you must give the new IBAN to every provider yourself, and while a few let you change details online, others only accept the change from the customer directly, sometimes just by recorded phone call. Keep a buffer in the account as well, since a bounced debit can mean return fees and eventually cut services. List every mandate before you switch, then work through it provider by provider.

frozen_account_en:
A Spanish bank account can be blocked while you are 2,000 km away.
Banks freeze accounts under anti-money-laundering rules, and the warning letters usually arrive by post, in Spanish, at your Spanish address, which is why so many owners only find out when the card stops working. An expired passport is the most common trigger and the easiest fix: send updated documents and the account usually reopens within days.
The serious causes are unpaid taxes, IBI included, where the tax agency can freeze the account through court-ordered debt collection, and missed loan payments. Unusual transfers can also trip the fraud filters, so tell your bank before a large or out-of-pattern payment such as a property purchase. Give the bank a current email address, keep every ID document valid, and have someone check the mailbox.

buying_documents_en:
In Spain you do not just buy the property. You buy everything owed on it.
Unpaid IBI, community fees and mortgages stay attached to the home, which is why the Nota Simple, around €10 online, is the first document to order. Next comes the NIE: pay the small fee at a bank branch with form 790 before your appointment and bring the stamped form, because the police station rarely takes payment. Non-EU citizens, including Brits, face longer waits now, so start early.
Then assemble the rest: a passport with at least six months left, proof of funds such as tax returns, payslips and bank statements, and a Spanish bank account, since taxes and most utilities are paid through one. When you make the offer, expect a modest reserve fee, refundable if the sale falls through, before the 10% arras deposit. Gather the paperwork before the property search, not during it.

offer_accepted_en:
An accepted offer in Spain means less than you think.
Until the arras contract is signed, nothing is binding and the seller can still take a better offer. The offer stage usually involves a reservation contract and a modest holding fee, refundable if the sale falls through, but it is the arras that changes everything: pull out and you lose the 10% deposit, while a seller who quits pays you double. You get the contract a few days early, so have a lawyer read it before signing.
From there, expect six to ten weeks to keys, with the completion date fixed in the arras itself. If you need a mortgage, the FEIN adds a mandatory 10-day reflection period, so the timeline is tighter than it looks. Get your NIE, Spanish bank account and funds ready before you bid, not after.

late_tax_penalties_en:
Missed a Spanish tax deadline? Moving first is worth real money.
If you file voluntarily before any letter arrives, the surcharge starts at 1% plus 1% for each month of delay, reaching 15% plus interest once you pass a year. Wait until the tax office contacts you and proper penalties apply instead, which can add at least half of the tax owed on top of the original bill. The same logic covers mistakes: a complementary return filed before any notification keeps corrections cheap.
The non-resident tax runs on its own quiet schedule, due by 31 December the following year, which is exactly why so many owners miss it. If the catch-up sum is uncomfortable, an instalment plan can be requested from the tax agency, though interest still runs. File first, then fix. Catching up is usually straightforward.
